cards.front: What line is the starting line for every bearing?

options.explanation: Every bearing starts from the North line at the point where the angle is measured. The angle is then measured clockwise from this line.
Using South as the starting line confuses bearings with some descriptions of direction. Every bearing begins at the North line and is measured clockwise.
East corresponds to a bearing of 090°, but it is not the starting line. Bearings always begin from the North line before turning clockwise.
West corresponds to a bearing of 270°, rather than the starting line. Every bearing is measured clockwise from the North line.

cards.front: A bearing is measured from [ ___ ] and goes [ ___ ].
cards.back: A bearing is measured from North and goes clockwise.

options.text: A bearing is measured from North and goes clockwise.
options.explanation: The standard convention for bearings is to begin at the North line and measure the angle clockwise. This ensures that each direction has one unambiguous bearing.

options.text: A bearing is measured from South and goes clockwise.
options.explanation: Starting from South uses the wrong reference line. A bearing is measured from North and goes clockwise, regardless of the direction of travel.

options.text: A bearing is measured from North and goes anticlockwise.
options.explanation: Measuring anticlockwise reverses the standard bearing convention. A bearing begins at North and goes clockwise around the point where the angle is measured.

options.text: A bearing is measured from East and goes anticlockwise.
options.explanation: This changes both parts of the bearing convention. Bearings are measured from North, not East, and turn clockwise rather than anticlockwise.

cards.front: In the bearing of B from A, which point is the angle measured at?

options.explanation: The phrase “B from A” means the journey or direction starts at A. Therefore, the bearing angle is drawn and measured at A.
Choosing B reverses the order of the bearing. In “the bearing of B from A”, A is the starting point, so the angle is measured at A.
The angle is not measured halfway between the points. The word “from” identifies A as the starting point, so the bearing angle is measured at A.
Bearings in opposite directions are generally different, so the angle cannot be measured at either point. “B from A” specifically requires measurement at A.

cards.front: What does the word from tell you in a bearing question?

options.explanation: The word “from” identifies the point where the bearing begins. The North line and the clockwise angle must therefore be drawn at that starting point.
Confusing “from” with the destination reverses the bearing. “From” identifies the starting point where the North line and bearing angle are drawn.
North is the reference direction for every bearing, but it is not identified by the word “from”. “From” tells you the starting point for measuring.
Bearings are measured clockwise, but the word “from” does not specify the angle. It identifies the starting point where that clockwise angle is measured.

cards.front: Bearings are written using [ ___ ], so 67° is written as [ ___ ].
cards.back: Bearings are written using three figures, so 67° is written as 067°.

options.text: Bearings are written using three figures, so 67° is written as 067°.
options.explanation: Bearings must contain three figures. Since 67 has only two figures, a zero is placed at the front to give the bearing 067°.

options.text: Bearings are written using two figures, so 67° is written as 67°.
options.explanation: Leaving 67° as two figures ignores the standard notation for bearings. Bearings use three figures, so a leading zero is required and the answer is 067°.

options.text: Bearings are written using three figures, so 67° is written as 670°.
options.explanation: Appending a zero changes the angle from 67° to 670°, which is not a valid single-turn bearing. Add the zero at the front to obtain 067°.

options.text: Bearings are written using four figures, so 67° is written as 0067°.
options.explanation: Four-figure notation adds an unnecessary leading zero. Bearings use exactly three figures, so 67° needs only one zero at the front: 067°.

cards.front: Write 7° as a three-figure bearing.

options.explanation: A bearing must be written with three figures. The angle 7° therefore needs two leading zeros, giving the three-figure bearing 007°.
Placing only one zero before 7 and another after it changes the angle to 70°. Two leading zeros are needed, so 7° is written 007°.
Adding zeros after the 7 changes the value to 700°, rather than formatting 7°. Leading zeros preserve the angle, giving the bearing 007°.
Adding 1 at the front changes the angle by 100°. A three-figure bearing uses leading zeros without changing its value, so 7° becomes 007°.

cards.front: Write 42° as a three-figure bearing.

options.explanation: The angle 42° has two figures, so one leading zero is added to make a three-figure bearing. This gives 042° without changing the angle.
Putting the zero after 42 multiplies the angle by ten and produces more than a full turn. The zero must go in front, giving 042°.
Placing the zero between 4 and 2 changes the value to 402°. A leading zero preserves the original 42° angle, so the bearing is 042°.
Adding 1 to the front changes the angle by 100°. Only a leading zero can complete the three-figure format without changing 42°, giving 042°.

cards.front: Why is 58° written as 058° for a bearing?

options.explanation: Standard bearing notation always uses three figures. Since 58 has only two figures, a leading zero is added to write the bearing as 058°.
Two figures would leave the angle as 58°, which does not follow standard bearing notation. Bearings require three figures, so it must be written as 058°.
Bearings do not use four-figure angle notation. They require exactly three figures, so 58° takes one leading zero and becomes 058°.
A trailing zero would change 58° into 580°, rather than simply formatting it. Bearings need three figures, so the zero is placed in front: 058°.

cards.front: If a bearing has fewer than three digits, add [ ___ ] at the [ ___ ].
cards.back: If a bearing has fewer than three digits, add leading zeros at the front.

options.text: If a bearing has fewer than three digits, add leading zeros at the front.
options.explanation: Bearings are always written using three digits, so zeros are placed before a shorter bearing. For example, a bearing of 45° is written as 045°.

options.text: If a bearing has fewer than three digits, add trailing zeros at the back.
options.explanation: Adding zeros at the end changes the angle, turning 45° into 450°. The correct convention is to add leading zeros at the front, giving 045°.

options.text: If a bearing has fewer than three digits, add leading zeros at the back.
options.explanation: Leading zeros belong before the existing digits, not after them. A two-digit bearing such as 45° must therefore be written as 045°.

options.text: If a bearing has fewer than three digits, add trailing zeros at the front.
options.explanation: Trailing zeros would alter the value of the bearing rather than standardise its notation. Bearings use leading zeros at the front until three digits are shown.

cards.front: What tool is used to measure or draw bearing angles?

options.explanation: A protractor has a marked angular scale, allowing bearing angles to be measured or drawn accurately in degrees from a North line.
A compass draws circles or arcs but does not have a degree scale for measuring angles. Bearing angles are measured or drawn using a protractor.
A ruler is useful for drawing straight direction lines, but it cannot measure angles in degrees. A protractor is required to measure or construct a bearing.
A set square provides only certain fixed angles, so it cannot measure arbitrary bearings. A protractor supplies the degree scale needed for bearing angles.

cards.front: When drawing a bearing, what should you draw before measuring the angle?

options.explanation: A bearing is measured clockwise from North, so a North line through the starting point must be drawn first as the reference direction.
An East line represents 090°, but it is not the starting reference for bearings. Draw a North line first because bearings are measured clockwise from North.
A South line represents 180° from North and is not the standard reference direction. Bearings must begin from a North line at the starting point.
A West line represents 270°, so using it as the initial reference shifts every measured angle. Bearings are measured clockwise from a North line.

cards.front: When drawing a bearing, what should 0° on the protractor line up with?

options.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise starting from North, so the protractor’s 0° mark must align with the North line through the relevant point.
East corresponds to a bearing of 090°, not the zero position. The protractor’s 0° mark must line up with North before measuring clockwise.
The direction line shows the final bearing rather than its starting reference. The 0° mark must align with the North line, from which the angle is measured.
The protractor’s curved edge contains the degree scale and cannot serve as the zero reference. Align 0° with the straight North line through the point.

cards.front: A bearing of 120° is more than [ ___ ] but less than [ ___ ].
cards.back: A bearing of 120° is more than 90° but less than 180°.

options.text: A bearing of 120° is more than 90° but less than 180°.
options.explanation: Since 120 lies between 90 and 180, this bearing points into the quadrant between East and South when measured clockwise from North.

options.text: A bearing of 120° is more than 120° but less than 180°.
options.explanation: Although 120° is less than 180°, it is equal to 120°, not more than it. The correct bounding angles are 90° and 180°.

options.text: A bearing of 120° is more than 90° but less than 120°.
options.explanation: A strict inequality cannot say that 120° is less than itself. The bearing is more than 90° and less than 180°.

options.text: A bearing of 120° is more than 180° but less than 270°.
options.explanation: A bearing of 120° has not passed 180°, so it cannot lie between 180° and 270°. It lies between 90° and 180°.

cards.front: A bearing of 120° from P points in which general direction?
cards.back: Down and to the right of P.

options.text: Down and to the right of P.
options.explanation: From North, turning 120° clockwise passes East at 90° and continues towards South. The resulting direction is therefore down and to the right of P.

options.text: Up and to the right of P.
options.explanation: Up and to the right corresponds to a clockwise bearing between 000° and 090°. Since 120° is between 090° and 180°, it points down and right.

options.text: Down and to the left of P.
options.explanation: Down and to the left corresponds to bearings between 180° and 270°. A bearing of 120° lies between East and South, so it points down and right.

options.text: Up and to the left of P.
options.explanation: Up and to the left corresponds to bearings between 270° and 360°. A 120° clockwise turn from North instead points down and to the right.

cards.front: If a diagram shows a small angle anticlockwise from North, is that angle the bearing?

options.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise from North. An angle marked anticlockwise is therefore not itself the bearing and must be subtracted from 360°.
The marked angle is measured in the wrong rotational direction. Bearings always go clockwise from North, so an anticlockwise angle must be converted using 360° minus the angle.
Bearings do start from North, but they must be measured clockwise rather than anticlockwise. The marked angle is converted by subtracting it from 360°.

options.text: Yes - bearings use the smaller angle.
options.explanation: Bearing conventions require clockwise measurement, not whichever rotation is shorter. A small anticlockwise angle is therefore not the bearing; its corresponding bearing is close to 360°.

cards.front: For a marked anticlockwise angle from North, bearing = [ ___ ] - [ ___ ].
cards.back: For a marked anticlockwise angle from North, bearing = 360° - marked angle.

options.text: For a marked anticlockwise angle from North, bearing = 360° - marked angle.
options.explanation: A full turn is 360°, so the remaining clockwise angle equals 360° minus the marked anticlockwise angle. This gives the required three-figure bearing.

options.text: For a marked anticlockwise angle from North, bearing = 180° - marked angle.
options.explanation: Subtracting from 180° treats the diagram as a half-turn and produces the wrong direction. The full angle around a point is 360°, so subtract from 360°.

options.text: For a marked anticlockwise angle from North, bearing = 360° + marked angle.
options.explanation: Adding the anticlockwise angle to 360° produces an angle greater than one complete turn. The clockwise bearing is the remainder, found using 360° minus the marked angle.

options.text: For a marked anticlockwise angle from North, bearing = marked angle - 360°.
options.explanation: Reversing the subtraction gives a negative value for any ordinary marked angle below 360°. The positive clockwise bearing is 360° minus the marked angle.

cards.front: A line is 35° anticlockwise from North. What is its bearing?

options.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise from North. Turning 35° anticlockwise is equivalent to turning 360° - 35° = 325° clockwise, giving a bearing of 325°.
This treats the 35° turn as clockwise rather than anticlockwise. Bearings are measured clockwise from North, so the correct calculation is 360° - 35° = 325°.
This incorrectly adds 180° as though finding a reverse bearing. The line is 35° anticlockwise from North, so its clockwise bearing is 360° - 35° = 325°.
This does not represent a 35° anticlockwise turn from North. Converting to the required clockwise angle gives 360° - 35° = 325°, so the bearing is 325°.

cards.front: What does a reverse bearing point compared with the original bearing?

options.explanation: A reverse bearing describes travel back along the same straight line, so it points in the direction exactly opposite to the original bearing.
Keeping the same direction leaves the original bearing unchanged. A reverse bearing points back along the same line in the opposite direction, differing by 180°.
All bearings are measured clockwise from North, but that does not define a reverse bearing. A reverse bearing points in the opposite direction along the same line.
A reverse bearing does not necessarily point North; its direction depends on the original journey. It points exactly opposite to the original bearing along the same line.

cards.front: Opposite directions differ by [ ___ ].

options.explanation: A full turn is 360°, so directions pointing exactly opposite each other are separated by half a turn, which is 180°.
A difference of 90° describes perpendicular directions, not opposite ones. Opposite directions are separated by half of a 360° turn, so they differ by 180°.
A 360° turn returns to the same direction rather than the opposite direction. Half a full turn is required, so opposite directions differ by 180°.
Although 270° clockwise reaches the same orientation as 90° anticlockwise, that is a quarter-turn relationship. Exactly opposite directions differ by 180°.

cards.front: How do you find a reverse bearing when the original bearing is less than 180°?

options.explanation: Reverse bearings differ by 180°. When the original bearing is below 180°, adding 180° produces the opposite direction while keeping the result below 360°.
Subtracting 180° from a bearing below 180° gives a negative angle. The reverse bearing is found by adding 180°, producing a valid three-figure bearing.
Adding 360° produces the same direction because it represents one complete turn. A reverse bearing points oppositely, so 180° must be added instead.
Subtracting the bearing from 360° reflects the direction around North rather than reversing it. For an original bearing below 180°, add 180°.

cards.front: How do you find a reverse bearing when the original bearing is more than 180°?

options.explanation: Reverse bearings differ by 180°. When the original bearing exceeds 180°, subtracting 180° gives the opposite direction as a valid bearing between 000° and 180°.
Adding 180° to a bearing above 180° produces a value over 360° unless another adjustment is made. The direct method is to subtract 180°.
Subtracting 360° represents a complete turn and therefore leaves the direction unchanged. To point in the opposite direction, subtract 180° from the original bearing.
Subtracting the bearing from 360° gives its reflection around the North line, not necessarily its reverse. For a bearing above 180°, subtract 180°.

cards.front: A journey from V to T has bearing 072°. What is the reverse bearing?

options.explanation: The original bearing 072° is below 180°, so adding 180° gives the opposite direction: 072° + 180° = 252°.
This comes from subtracting 072° from 180°, which finds a supplementary angle but not the reverse bearing. Add 180° to 072° to obtain 252°.
This comes from calculating 360° - 072°, which reflects the bearing around North rather than reversing the journey. The reverse is 072° + 180° = 252°.
This results from an addition error when combining 072° and 180°. Reverse bearings differ by exactly 180°, so the correct total is 252°.

cards.front: A journey from A to B has bearing 230°. What is the reverse bearing?

options.explanation: The original bearing 230° is above 180°, so subtracting 180° gives the reverse direction: 230° - 180° = 050°, written with three figures.
This subtracts 100° rather than the required half-turn. Reverse bearings differ by 180°, so 230° - 180° = 050°.
This adds 80° rather than reversing the direction by half a turn. Since 230° exceeds 180°, subtract 180° to obtain 050°.
This results from a subtraction error when calculating 230° - 180°. The difference is 50°, which must be written as the three-figure bearing 050°.
